lines.text: Here's a table of two million orders, and one query: count a customer's orders, and add up the amounts.
lines.caption: Here's a table of two million orders, and one query: count a customer's orders, and add up the amounts.

lines.text: For customer forty-two forty-two, it takes fifteen microseconds to execute.
lines.caption: For customer 4242, it takes fifteen microseconds to execute.

lines.text: For customer one, it takes a hundred and thirty-five milliseconds.
lines.caption: For customer one, it takes a hundred and thirty-five milliseconds.

lines.text: About nine thousand times longer.
lines.caption: About nine thousand times longer.

lines.text: Same query, same table, same machine.
lines.caption: Same query, same table, same machine.

lines.text: And nothing in the query says how to run it.
lines.caption: And nothing in the query says how to run it.

lines.text: So who decides?
lines.caption: So who decides?

lines.text: And why is the same query sometimes fast, and sometimes slow?
lines.caption: And why is the same query sometimes fast, and sometimes slow?

lines.text: In ordinary code, you'd write the search yourself: loop over every order, and keep the ones for this customer.
lines.caption: In ordinary code, you'd write the search yourself: loop over every order, and keep the ones for this customer.

lines.text: The code says exactly how.
lines.caption: The code says exactly how.

lines.text: sequel is declarative.
lines.caption: SQL is declarative.

lines.text: The query says what rows you want, and nothing about how to find them.
lines.caption: The query says what rows you want, and nothing about how to find them.

lines.text: That leaves the database free to choose how.
lines.caption: That leaves the database free to choose how.

lines.text: And it has to choose, every time the query runs.
lines.caption: And it has to choose, every time the query runs.

segments.title: Two ways to find the rows

lines.text: The table is stored in pages, blocks of about a hundred and sixty rows each.
lines.caption: The table is stored in pages, blocks of about a hundred and sixty rows each.

lines.text: Two million orders fill about twelve thousand seven hundred of them.
lines.caption: Two million orders fill about twelve thousand seven hundred of them.

lines.text: There are two basic ways to find one customer's orders.
lines.caption: There are two basic ways to find one customer's orders.

lines.text: One is a full scan: read every page, and keep the rows that match.
lines.caption: One is a full scan: read every page, and keep the rows that match.

lines.text: It reads the same pages whoever the customer is.
lines.caption: It reads the same pages whoever the customer is.

lines.text: The other is an index: a sorted list of customer numbers, each pointing to where that customer's rows are.
lines.caption: The other is an index: a sorted list of customer numbers, each pointing to where that customer's rows are.

lines.text: Find the customer in the list, collect where their rows are, and read only the pages that hold them.
lines.caption: Find the customer in the list, collect where their rows are, and read only the pages that hold them.

lines.text: Customer forty-two forty-two has ten orders, on ten pages.
lines.caption: Customer 4242 has ten orders, on ten pages.

lines.text: Through the index, that's ten pages instead of twelve thousand seven hundred.
lines.caption: Through the index, that's ten pages instead of twelve thousand seven hundred.

lines.text: Customer one has about six hundred thousand orders.
lines.caption: Customer one has about six hundred thousand orders.

lines.text: Orders are stored in the order they arrived, not by customer, so on every page, about three rows in ten are customer one's.
lines.caption: Orders are stored in the order they arrived, not by customer, so on every page, about three rows in ten are customer one's.

lines.text: Now the index can't skip anything.
lines.caption: Now the index can't skip anything.

lines.text: Every page has to be read anyway.
lines.caption: Every page has to be read anyway.

lines.text: So whether the index saves work depends on how many rows match.
lines.caption: So whether the index saves work depends on how many rows match.

lines.text: And that depends on the customer.
lines.caption: And that depends on the customer.

lines.text: The choice between them is made by the query planner.
lines.caption: The choice between them is made by the query planner.

lines.text: The planner keeps statistics about each table: how many rows it has, and for each column, which values are most common, and how common.
lines.caption: The planner keeps statistics about each table: how many rows it has, and for each column, which values are most common, and how common.

lines.text: For each way it could run the query, it estimates the rows and pages it would touch, turns that into a cost, a number for comparing plans rather than a time, and picks the cheapest.
lines.caption: For each way it could run the query, it estimates the rows and pages it would touch, turns that into a cost, a number for comparing plans rather than a time, and picks the cheapest.

lines.text: For customer forty-two forty-two, the statistics say rare.
lines.caption: For customer 4242, the statistics say rare.

lines.text: The planner estimates thirty-three rows; the real number is ten, close enough to choose well.
lines.caption: The planner estimates thirty-three rows; the real number is ten, close enough to choose well.

lines.text: Its cost for using the index comes to about a hundred and thirty; for a full scan, about thirty-eight thousand.
lines.caption: Its cost for using the index comes to about a hundred and thirty; for a full scan, about thirty-eight thousand.

lines.text: So it picks the index, read the way we just saw: collect the rows' locations, sort them by page, then read each of those pages once.
lines.caption: So it picks the index, read the way we just saw: collect the rows' locations, sort them by page, then read each of those pages once.

lines.text: Postgres Q L calls that a bitmap scan, shown as two steps: one reads the index, the other reads the pages.
lines.caption: PostgreSQL calls that a bitmap scan, shown as two steps: one reads the index, the other reads the pages.

lines.text: Ten pages, fifteen microseconds.
lines.caption: Ten pages, fifteen microseconds.

lines.text: Force a full scan for the same customer, and it takes seventy-two milliseconds: nearly five thousand times slower.
lines.caption: Force a full scan for the same customer, and it takes seventy-two milliseconds: nearly five thousand times slower.

lines.text: The choice matters.
lines.caption: The choice matters.

lines.text: For customer one, the statistics say about three in ten orders.
lines.caption: For customer one, the statistics say about three in ten orders.

lines.text: The planner estimates about six hundred thousand rows, and picks the same kind of bitmap scan.
lines.caption: The planner estimates about six hundred thousand rows, and picks the same kind of bitmap scan.

lines.text: But this time the pages it reads are all of them.
lines.caption: But this time the pages it reads are all of them.

lines.text: A hundred and thirty-five milliseconds.
lines.caption: A hundred and thirty-five milliseconds.

lines.text: Force a full scan instead, and it's no faster: it reads the same pages, and still has six hundred thousand rows to add up.
lines.caption: Force a full scan instead, and it's no faster: it reads the same pages, and still has six hundred thousand rows to add up.

lines.text: When the rows you want are on every page, the index doesn't help, and no plan is fast.
lines.caption: When the rows you want are on every page, the index doesn't help, and no plan is fast.

lines.text: Everything so far read one table.
lines.caption: Everything so far read one table.

lines.text: Now ask for the orders of every customer in Tromso.
lines.caption: Now ask for the orders of every customer in Tromsø.

lines.text: Two tables have to meet, and the planner has to choose how to match their rows.
lines.caption: Two tables have to meet, and the planner has to choose how to match their rows.

lines.text: A hundred customers live in Tromso, out of a hundred thousand.
lines.caption: A hundred customers live in Tromsø, out of a hundred thousand.

lines.text: The planner finds those hundred customers, then, for each one, looks up its orders in the index.
lines.caption: The planner finds those hundred customers, then, for each one, looks up its orders in the index.

lines.text: That's a nested loop: for each row on one side, look up its matches on the other.
lines.caption: That's a nested loop: for each row on one side, look up its matches on the other.

lines.text: About five milliseconds.
lines.caption: About five milliseconds.

lines.text: Now ask for customers in Oslo: almost all of the hundred thousand.
lines.caption: Now ask for customers in Oslo: almost all of the hundred thousand.

lines.text: This time the planner builds a lookup table from the Oslo customers, and streams all two million orders through it, once.
lines.caption: This time the planner builds a lookup table from the Oslo customers, and streams all two million orders through it, once.

lines.text: That's a hash join.
lines.caption: That's a hash join.

lines.text: About seven hundred milliseconds, for almost two million rows.
lines.caption: About seven hundred milliseconds, for almost two million rows.

lines.text: Force a nested loop for Oslo instead, and it takes two seconds: nearly three times as long.
lines.caption: Force a nested loop for Oslo instead, and it takes two seconds: nearly three times as long.

lines.text: Same query shape.
lines.caption: Same query shape.

lines.text: A different plan, because a different number of rows match.
lines.caption: A different plan, because a different number of rows match.

lines.text: The plan is only as good as the estimate, and the statistics are a snapshot.
lines.caption: The plan is only as good as the estimate, and the statistics are a snapshot.

lines.text: Here's a copy of the orders table.
lines.caption: Here's a copy of the orders table.

lines.text: Its statistics were gathered while customer one still had three in ten orders.
lines.caption: Its statistics were gathered while customer one still had three in ten orders.

lines.text: Since then, their older orders were archived, and just two hundred and ninety-four are left, all of them recent.
lines.caption: Since then, their older orders were archived, and just two hundred and ninety-four are left, all of them recent.

lines.text: Now ask for customer one's first ten orders, by order number.
lines.caption: Now ask for customer one's first ten orders, by order number.

lines.text: The planner still believes customer one is everywhere: about four hundred and twenty thousand rows.
lines.caption: The planner still believes customer one is everywhere: about four hundred and twenty thousand rows.

lines.text: So it walks through the orders by order number, expecting to run into ten of theirs almost at once.
lines.caption: So it walks through the orders by order number, expecting to run into ten of theirs almost at once.

lines.text: But all of theirs are at the very end.
lines.caption: But all of theirs are at the very end.

lines.text: It passes about one point four million other rows first.
lines.caption: It passes about one point four million other rows first.

lines.text: A hundred and thirty-seven milliseconds.
lines.caption: A hundred and thirty-seven milliseconds.

lines.text: Run analyze, which refreshes the statistics, and the planner now expects about three hundred and thirty rows.
lines.caption: Run ANALYZE, which refreshes the statistics, and the planner now expects about three hundred and thirty rows.

lines.text: It looks them up in the index, sorts them, and keeps the first ten.
lines.caption: It looks them up in the index, sorts them, and keeps the first ten.

lines.text: Sixty microseconds: more than two thousand times faster, for the same query.
lines.caption: Sixty microseconds: more than two thousand times faster, for the same query.

lines.text: The usual fix for a slow query is to add an index.
lines.caption: The usual fix for a slow query is to add an index.

lines.text: But nobody added one here: the one on customer number was there all along.
lines.caption: But nobody added one here: the one on customer number was there all along.

lines.text: The planner just didn't expect it to help.
lines.caption: The planner just didn't expect it to help.

lines.text: That's how to read a slow plan.
lines.caption: That's how to read a slow plan.

lines.text: explain analyze shows, for each step, the rows the planner expected and the rows it actually got.
lines.caption: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows, for each step, the rows the planner expected and the rows it actually got.

lines.text: Where the two are far apart, the plan was chosen for data that isn't there.
lines.caption: Where the two are far apart, the plan was chosen for data that isn't there.

lines.text: So who decides how a query runs?
lines.caption: So who decides how a query runs?

lines.text: The query planner, because sequel only says what you want.
lines.caption: The query planner, because SQL only says what you want.

lines.text: It weighs the ways it could run the query by how many rows and pages each step will touch, using statistics about your data.
lines.caption: It weighs the ways it could run the query by how many rows and pages each step will touch, using statistics about your data.

lines.text: A rare customer gets the index, and ten pages.
lines.caption: A rare customer gets the index, and ten pages.

lines.text: For a common one, every page has to be read, whatever the plan.
lines.caption: For a common one, every page has to be read, whatever the plan.

lines.text: A few matches, with an index to look them up, get a nested loop; many get a hash join.
lines.caption: A few matches, with an index to look them up, get a nested loop; many get a hash join.

lines.text: That's why the same query can be fast or slow: it depends on the data it touches, and on what the planner believes about that data.
lines.caption: That's why the same query can be fast or slow: it depends on the data it touches, and on what the planner believes about that data.

lines.text: When a query is slow, don't guess, and don't just add an index.
lines.caption: When a query is slow, don't guess, and don't just add an index.

lines.text: Run explain analyze, and compare the rows the planner expected with the rows it got.
lines.caption: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and compare the rows the planner expected with the rows it got.
